r1: Heading aligned to the body term 'mokedikedi o rothang'.

r2: DISPUTE: the problem is only partly real. 'o rothang' means flowing or dripping (not rotting), so the heading does say liquid that drains out; the 'rotting' reading is a blind back-translator slip. 'Mokedikedi' is the term the deck's s17 quiz already uses for the leachate liquid (draft file lines 108 and 113, 'mokedikedi o rothang ho tswa moqomong'). I could not verify the proposed spelling 'mokelikeli', so I did not change this heading alone and create an inconsistency within the slide. If a facilitator confirms 'mokelikeli' as the correct spelling, change it in all three places together. Heading is 37 characters, within the 45 limit.

opus accepted: I'm accepting the current wording, but this is my own judgement and nobody has checked it. 'Mokedikedi' is the word South African Sesotho school glossaries use for 'liquid', as in solid, liquid and gas. So it is not a misspelling of 'mokelikeli'. 'O rothang' comes from -rotha, 'to drip'. Together they mean 'liquid that drips out', which fits 'liquid drainage'. The 'rotting' reading came from the back-translator. Keeping this wording also matches the slide's quiz, which uses 'mokedikedi o rothang ho tswa moqomong'. Worm Castings stays in English, which the rules allow. The heading is 37 characters, under the 45 limit, and nothing is added or left out. If a facilitator confirms a different spelling, change it in all three places on slide 17 at once.

reasons: Soil becomes 'mavu' and bare ground becomes 'mavu a songo fukwaho', following the learner mulch wording and the deck's other units. I translated 'safe' as 'i si na khombo' (without danger) and put '(safe)' after it, because this is a safety meaning and the earlier 'yo tsireledzeaho' reads as 'protected'. I dropped 'tsimu dza zwivhungu' (crop fields of worms) and kept 'worm farms' in English, matching s17.p0 and the learner Soil key point. 'cover crops' also stays in English. checkRounds.backTranslation: In this module, learn to read soil, to make compost that has no danger (safe), to protect soil that is not covered, and to use cover crops and worm farms.

problems.issue: The repair fixes the open problem (soil, safe and bare ground are now translated, and the wrong 'tsimu dza zwivhungu' is gone). No meaning is lost or changed. Three small defects remain. (1) The English gloss '(safe)' still sits after 'i si na khombo'. 'safe' is an ordinary word and the Venda alone already carries it, so the bracket should be dropped. (2) 'worm farms' and 'cover crops' stay in English. They fit grammatically after 'na', but the replacement for the bad 'tsimu dza zwivhungu' is just English, and a Tshivenda gloss or descriptor would serve farmers better. (3) 'u ita compost i si na khombo' is a slightly clumsy relative construction; 'ine ya si na khombo' would be smoother.

revisionNotes: module = tshipiḓa tsha pfunzo (part of the course), soil/bare ground/worm farms translated (zwivhungu follows the learner draft). compost matches the body of the deck.

targetFieldChanges.sourceEnglish: If your compost smells of ammonia and feels slimy, add dry carbon such as straw and turn it.

currentTarget.text: Arali compost yaṋu i tshi nukha ammonia nahone ni tshi i fara ya vha slimy, shelani carbon yo omaho u fana na straw nahone ni i rembuluse.
currentTarget.provenance: Bounded deck-only machine draft (Soil/Water ordinary-prose completion, 4–5 October 2026): drafted, blind back-translated and semantically checked by separate AI agents; difficult technical English retained. Unreviewed; not fluent or local farming approval.

targetFieldChanges.backTranslation: If your compost is smelling of ammonia and when you hold it it is slimy, add dry carbon like straw and turn it.

reasons: The guidance says to keep 'slimy' and 'straw' in English, as the course's learner wording does. The ungrammatical 'i tshi pfala i slimy' is replaced by the construction from s11.p1, 'ya vha slimy' (= 'it is slimy'). 'feels' is kept by framing the condition as touch: 'ni tshi i fara ya vha slimy' (= 'when you hold or touch it, it is slimy'). The deck already uses 'fara' for feeling soil by hand (s07.p1 'ni fare mavu'), so the sense of touch comes through on a verb we are confident of, not on the unrecovered 'pfala'. Both conditions are joined by 'nahone' ('and'), not 'kana' ('or'). 'yo omaho' (dry) stays attached to carbon, following 'browns dzo omaho' (s10.p0) and 'hatsi ho omaho' (s15.p0). No grass or other material is added. Both actions stay in order: 'shelani' (add) and then 'nahone ni i rembuluse' (and turn it), as in s11.p1. A facilitator may wish to confirm that the 'fara' framing reads naturally as 'feels'.

checkRounds.text: Arali compost yaṋu i tshi nukha ammonia nahone ni tshi i fara ya vha slimy, shelani carbon yo omaho u fana na straw nahone ni i rembuluse.
checkRounds.backTranslation: If your compost is smelling of ammonia and when you hold it it is slimy, add dry carbon like straw and turn it.

problems.issue: No critical or major problem. Both conditions are joined by 'nahone'. 'Dry' ('yo omaho'), the material (carbon, straw), the actions (add, then turn) and their order all match the English. 'Slimy' is retained deliberately. The five retained English words sit in grammatical slots ('nukha ammonia', 'ya vha slimy', 'u fana na straw'), and 'carbon' is the object of 'shelani'. 'Feels' comes through only approximately. 'ni tshi i fara' is back-translated as 'when you hold it', which is a grip or handling verb rather than a plain 'feels'. It still reads as a tactile check, so the meaning holds. The reviewer may want to confirm that 'u fara' and the 'ya vha slimy' predicate sound natural, since 'i tshi vha slimy' might read more smoothly. This is awkwardness, not a meaning change.

revisionNotes: Terms and wording consistent with s11.p1 and s15.p0.

revisionNotes: 45 characters. 'Swikhwama swa mbewu' (pouches of seed) is my rendering of seed pods; not an established term, flag for review.

r1: Real: 'swikhwama' = bags. 'swikhumba swa mbewu' (pods/husks of seed) is the checker's candidate, but 'xikhumba' also means bark (s13.p1), so facilitators must confirm the pod word. 'Thyaka' (dirt) replaced by 'swithyakisi' (things that contaminate), consistent with 'thyakisiwangi' in s13.p1. Length is 50 chars, slightly over the 45 aim. Apply the same pod word in s13.p0, which is not in this batch.

r2: Real problem. "Swikhumba swa Mbewu" meant seed skins or peels, so the referent was wrong. "Seed pods" is now kept in English, as the deck already does elsewhere ("wattle seed pods", "seed pods"). "Swithyakisi" (contaminants) is kept from the draft because it was not disputed. "Swi tshike ehandle" (leave them outside) replaces "Hlayisa ... Ehandle", which could read as "store outside". The heading is 44 characters. Facilitators should confirm the wording.

opus accepted: I checked all three earlier fixes, and each one had a problem. 'Swikhwama swa mbewu' means 'bags of seed' and 'swikhumba swa mbewu' means 'seed skins/husks', so both point to the wrong thing. There is no confirmed Xitsonga word for a seed pod. Keeping 'seed pods' in English is defensible: this is a botanical term with no established target word, and the deck already uses it this way ('wattle seed pods', 'seed pods' in s13.p0). Keeping it the same as s13.p0 is better than bringing in an unconfirmed word that could mean something else. The heading is still grammatical. 'X ni swithyakisi: swi tshike ehandle' uses class 8 'swi' to agree with both nouns. 'Swi tshike ehandle' is a correct imperative with an object marker ('leave them outside') and keeps the 'keep out' meaning. At 44 characters it is within the length limit. A facilitator should still confirm whether a native word for 'pod' is in local use. The back-translation's '[?]' guesses ('handle', 'left behind') come from 'ehandle' being misread and do not show a real meaning error.

checkNotes: moderate: Unchanged clause 'a xi vhumbhi ndlela leyi mati ma nga ta famba ha yona ndhawini yo karhi' (EN 'it does not predict how water will move at a particular site') relies on 'vhumbhi', which is not a Xitsonga word for 'predict': the standard stem is 'vumba' (v-, not vh-) meaning make, form or shape (e.g. 01-what-is-permaculture.md:135 'swivumbeko swa ntumbuluko' = EN 'nature's shapes', 'mibhedhi leyi vumbiweke' = EN 'beds shaped like a spiral'), and the 'vh-' spelling matches Tshivenda 'vhumba' (create, shape). The only other 'vhumb-' verb in the course is 'a swi vhumbi mali leyi nghenaka' in the unreviewed market-community draft (EN 'does not predict income'), which is the same machine slip, not independent attestation. A Xitsonga reader gets 'it does not shape/form the way water moves', so the point of the disclaimer (do not use this picture to forecast water behaviour at a site) is garbled in a limits-of-the-diagram sentence. Pre-existing: not in a span the edit touched.

followUpEdits.by: main-loop repair (Opus) of an issue found by the independent six-lens audit; blind Sonnet back-translation; independent Sonnet check
followUpEdits.reason: Predict is "bvumba" in standard Xitsonga: Chapatte, Tsonga-English Dictionary, "-bvumba: guess, foretell, predict, prophesy". The course uses the same root for guessing: docs/narration/intro-permaculture.ts slide 10 "kumbe wa bvumbetela?" (or are you guessing?) and lib/course-translation-drafts-ts-market-community.ts "ematshan’wini yo byala hi ku bvumbha" (instead of planting by guessing). "vhumbhi" follows the Tshivenda verb "vhumba" (form, shape; content/manual/ve/07 "zwi vhumba tshiṱaṱo"); the Xitsonga form/create verb is "vumba". The six-lens audit found that a reader could take "a xi vhumbhi" as "it does not shape", losing the limit that the diagram is not a forecast for one site. The Market lesson writes "a swi vhumbi" for "do not predict"; that lesson is outside this batch and is noted for its owner.
followUpEdits.previousText: Loko mpfula yi ba mulch ematshan’wini ya misava leyi nga funengetiwangiki, matimba yo tala ya mathonsi ya mpfula ma hangalaka. Xifaniso lexi xi kombisa ntsena mhaka ya ku ba ka le vuandlalweni; a xi vhumbhi ndlela leyi mati ma nga ta famba ha yona ndhawini yo karhi.

A learner therefore reads “The instructions do not define every source in the same way”, which makes advisory guidance sound like binding orders. The wording is identical in previousText and newText, so the edit neither causes nor fixes it; the same noun recurs in the lesson (L128 next sentence “Ditaelo tsa Afrika Borwa…”, key point L130 “ditaelo tsa metsi a ditshila (greywater)”) and on slide 19 body[1], so it is a module-wide choice.

It means water coming out of the nappies (the course uses the same 'metsi a tswang' plus locative pattern for water leaving a place: "ke metsi a tswang matlwaneng" (st/07:384), EN 'Blackwater is water from toilets', and "a tswang bateng, shawareng le disinking" (st/01:124), EN 'used water from baths, showers and basins'), and it has no word for washing, so the blind reader reads it as nappy run-off. The direction of the prohibition is intact, but its scope can be under-read: a household whose nappy-wash water reaches a greywater system may think this line does not cover it. The course's own wording for the same English is 'metsi a ho hlatswa dinapi' ("Blackwater le metsi a ho hlatswa dinapi" (st/07:384), EN 'Blackwater and nappy water'; "metsi a kitjhene kapa a ho hlatswa dinapi" (st/01:124), EN 'kitchen or nappy water'; glossary "Metsi a tswang matlwaneng le a ho hlatswa dinapi" (st/12:15), EN 'Water from toilets and nappies'); 'metsi a tswang dinapining' has 0 [1 in excluded decks only] uses elsewhere. moderate: Pre-existing, unchanged span: 'Ditaelo' is too strong for 'guidance'. The blind reader back-translates it as 'instructions/directives (lit. commands)', so 'South African guidance differs' reads as 'South Africa's directives differ', which presents non-binding guidance as binding orders. In the course 'ditaelo' means instructions or orders ("Latela ditaelo tse pakeng" (st/05:96), EN 'Follow the instructions on the pack'; "Ditaelo tse netefaditsweng di fana ka tlhahisoleseding ka demand" (learner st-market-community) = 'Confirmed orders'), while guidance/guidelines is 'tataiso'/'ditataiso' ("Tsena ke ditataiso, e seng melao" (st/07:291), EN 'These are guidelines, not rules'; "sebedisa tataiso ya ho boloka peo e itseng ya sejalo ka seng" (learner st-seeds-sovereignty) = 'use crop-specific seed-saving guidance'; 'tataiso' 16 uses). The same slip is in the first paragraph of this slide (s19.p0, "Ditaelo ha di hlalose mohlodi o mong le o mong ka tsela e tshwanang", EN 'Guidance does not define every source in the same way') and 3 times in the learner water lesson (e.g. "Mehlodi ya metsi le ditaelo tsa metsi a ditshila (greywater) di ka fapana" (learner st-water-harvesting) = 'Water sources and greywater guidance can differ'), so these should be fixed together.

targetFieldChanges.sourceEnglish: Prevent contact with people or animals. Do not connect washwater to drinking-water plumbing, spray it, let it pool, or allow it to run off the property into a street, drain or watercourse.

currentTarget.text: Thibela hore batho kapa diphoofolo ba kopane le metsi ao. O se ke wa hokela metsi a sebedisitsweng ho hlatswa ho diphaephe tsa metsi a nowang, o se ke wa a fafatsa, o se ke wa a dumella ho ema kapa ho bokellana hodima lefatshe (pool), kapa o se ke wa a dumella hore a phalle ho tswa sebakeng sa hao ho ya seterateng, mokoting wa metsi (drain) kapa tseleng ya metsi a phallang (watercourse: noka, molatswana kapa kanale).
currentTarget.provenance: Bounded deck-only machine draft (Soil/Water ordinary-prose completion, 4–5 October 2026): drafted, blind back-translated and semantically checked by separate AI agents; difficult technical English retained. Unreviewed; not fluent or local farming approval.

targetFieldChanges.backTranslation: Prevent people or animals from coming into contact with that water. Do not connect water that has been used for washing to the pipes of drinking water, do not sprinkle it, do not allow it to stand or to gather on top of the ground (pool), or do not allow it to flow from your place to the street, to the water ditch (drain) or to the road of water that flows (watercourse: river, stream [?] or canal).

reasons: (1) Watercourse is now 'tseleng ya metsi a phallang' (a path of flowing water). It reads as one destination, and the bracket lists river, stream and channel as examples. That ends the narrowing to 'molatswana' (small stream) while the run-off ban still names exactly three destinations: street, drain and watercourse. It also matches the deck's s10.p2 precedent, which pairs noka/molatswana with (watercourse). (2) 'Let it pool' is now 'ho ema kapa ho bokellana hodima lefatshe (pool)': water standing or collecting on the ground. This replaces 'ho bopa matangwana', because 'matangwana' is the course word for built ponds. (3) 'Drain' gets an English bracket because 'mokoti wa metsi' may be read as a ditch or pit rather than a street or stormwater drain. All four bans keep their own 'o se ke wa'. The first sentence still means 'prevent contact between this water and people or animals'. The text runs about 2x the English length; safety completeness took priority.

checkRounds.text: Thibela hore batho kapa diphoofolo ba kopane le metsi ao. O se ke wa hokela metsi a sebedisitsweng ho hlatswa ho diphaephe tsa metsi a nowang, o se ke wa a fafatsa, o se ke wa a dumella ho ema kapa ho bokellana hodima lefatshe (pool), kapa o se ke wa a dumella hore a phalle ho tswa sebakeng sa hao ho ya seterateng, mokoting wa metsi (drain) kapa tseleng ya metsi a phallang (watercourse: noka, molatswana kapa kanale).
checkRounds.backTranslation: Prevent people or animals from coming into contact with that water. Do not connect water that has been used for washing to the pipes of drinking water, do not sprinkle it, do not allow it to stand or to gather on top of the ground (pool), or do not allow it to flow from your place to the street, to the water ditch (drain) or to the road of water that flows (watercourse: river, stream [?] or canal).

problems.issue: The first sentence says 'metsi ao' (that water), but washwater has not been named yet. The English 'Prevent contact' is also implicit, so the referent only becomes clear in the next sentence. Naming it up front would be clearer. This is not a meaning loss. Otherwise the draft is faithful. The first open problem is fixed: the watercourse ban now covers 'tseleng ya metsi a phallang (watercourse)' with noka, molatswana and kanale listed as examples, so molatswana no longer narrows it. The second is fixed: 'ho ema kapa ho bokellana hodima lefatshe (pool)' clearly means standing or gathering on the ground. All four prohibitions keep their scope and negation (connect to drinking-water plumbing, spray, pool, run off the property into a street, drain or watercourse). There is no ordinary English left, and the retained bracketed terms (pool, drain, watercourse) sit in grammatical sentences.

resolvedCheckerNotes: major/water-safety: "watercourse" is glossed with "molatswana", which means a small stream. English "watercourse" covers rivers, streams and channels, so the prohibition on run-off into a watercourse is narrowed in scope. The back-translation shows the narrowed reading ("small stream"). The English gloss in brackets does not fix this, because the native word is what the reader parses first.

major/water-safety: "let it pool" is rendered "ho bopa matangwana". The back-translator flagged "matangwana" as uncertain (puddles or small ponds), and "ho bopa" (to form or shape) is an odd collocation here. The pooling prohibition is a safety condition, so its meaning must be unambiguous. A facilitator should confirm the term.
revisionNotes: Full translation; watercourse as a bracketed gloss following the slide 10 precedent. Pooling rendered as ho bopa matangwana.

r1: Real, major: 'metsi a ho hlatswa' (water for washing) now 'metsi a sebedisitsweng ho hlatswa' (water already used for washing), matching the deck's 'metsi a sebedisitsweng'. 'Metsi a ditshila' removed from 'drain' so it is not narrowed to a sewage drain. 'Sebakeng sa hao' replaced with 'mobung wa hao' (your land). All five prohibitions are kept in scope.

r2: Real problem: the drinking-water-pipe prohibition was ambiguous ('washing and drinking-water pipes'). Now 'ho hlatswa ho diphaephe' clearly links washwater to the drinking-water plumbing, and the contact sentence names the water explicitly as the thing people and animals must not touch. 'mobung wa hao' (your soil) changed to 'sebakeng sa hao' (your property/site) to match 'property'.

opus: This is a safety prohibition, so each ban now repeats 'o se ke wa' and its negative scope is explicit. That rules out a 'not all together' reading. The destination list is reduced to the three English items: street, drain and 'molatswana (watercourse)'. The bracketed English keeps the term clear, and dropping 'tsela ya noka kapa' removes the apparent fourth item. The rest of the wording is kept verbatim. Length stays under 1.8 times the English.

targetFieldChanges.backTranslation: Take (pl.) the first water that is not clean [?] (Dirty First Flush) far from the tank.

reasons: The old verb 'Shandukisani' means change/replace, which lost the safety direction. 'Isani ... kule na Thanka' means 'take ... away from the tank', so it clearly says the dirty first flush is sent away and does not go into the tank. This is the action that s15.p0 and s16.p0 describe ('i thivhela ... uri a si dzhene kha thanka'). 'Kule na' is a common, unambiguous phrase for 'away from', so the heading does not depend on an uncertain verb and no '(divert)' gloss is needed. 'A thoma' (first) and 'a si kunaho' (dirty) are kept from the earlier draft. 'Thanka' matches the spelling in s16.h and s16.p0. The heading is about 45 characters.

The major problem was real. Bare 'a thoma' could be read as the verb 'begin', so I changed it to 'a u thoma', the usual Tshivenda form for the adjective 'first' ('the water of the beginning'). The relative 'a si kunaho' (that is not clean) now clearly describes that water. I kept the direction 'Isani ... kule na Thanka' (take it away from the tank) unchanged. On the minor problem: 'a si kunaho' is weaker than 'dirty', and 'first water' loses the sense of an initial surge. I was not confident a native word for 'dirty' carries the exact meaning, so I added '(Dirty First Flush)' in brackets. That follows the bracket rule and matches the deck, which keeps 'First Flush' in English on s16 and in the body text. A Venda speaker should still confirm this.

checkRounds.text: Isani Maḓi a Thoma a si Kunaho kule na Thanka
checkRounds.backTranslation: Come/Take [?] water, it does not begin/start to be [?] far from the tank

problems.issue: The open problem is fixed. 'Isani ... kule na Thanka' now means take it away from the tank, so the direction is kept. The modifier 'a thoma a si kunaho' is shaky, though. 'a thoma' reads as the verb 'begin', not the adjective 'first'. The blind back-translator did read it as a clause, 'it does not begin/start to be [?]'. That is a different meaning: water that has not started to be clean, not the first (dirty) water. The usual Venda form would be 'maḓi a u thoma' or 'a mathomo'. Suggest rewording to something like 'Isani maḓi a u thoma o ṱaha/a si kunaho kule na thanka', with 'first' as an adjective and a clear relative clause, ideally via a Venda speaker. This is a grammar and clarity risk, not a loss of the safety direction.

English 'Dirty' is rendered as the negative 'a si kunaho' (not clean/nice), which is weaker than 'dirty' (the back-translator also marked kunaho as [?]). 'First flush' is rendered as just 'first water', which loses the sense of an initial surge of roof runoff. The safety action still comes across, so this is awkwardness only.

targetFieldChanges.sourceEnglish: Prevent contact with people or animals. Do not connect washwater to drinking-water plumbing, spray it, let it pool, or allow it to run off the property into a street, drain or watercourse.

currentTarget.text: Thivhelani uri maḓi o shumiswaho u ṱanzwa (washwater) a kwame vhathu kana zwipuka (animals). Ni songo ṱumanya maḓi ayo na phaiphi dza maḓi a u nwa, ni songo a pfafadza (spray), ni songo tendela uri a ime fhethu huthihi a ite tshidziva (pool), kana ni songo tendela uri a elele a bva nga nnḓa ha mukano wa fhethu haṋu (property) a ye kha tshiṱaraṱa, kha mugero wa u bvisa maḓi (drain) kana kha nḓila ya maḓi a elelaho (watercourse).
currentTarget.provenance: Bounded deck-only machine draft (Soil/Water ordinary-prose completion, 4–5 October 2026): drafted, blind back-translated and semantically checked by separate AI agents; difficult technical English retained. Unreviewed; not fluent or local farming approval.

targetFieldChanges.backTranslation: Prevent (pl.) the water that has been used for washing (washwater) from touching people or animals. Do not (pl.) connect that water with drinking-water pipes (lit. 'pipes of water of to drink'), do not spray [?] it, do not allow it to stand in one place and form a pool, or do not allow it to flow out beyond the boundary [?] of your place (property) and go into the street, into a channel for removing water (drain) or into the route of flowing water (watercourse).

reasons: The back-translation read 'zwipuka' as 'plants', so 'animals' now reads 'zwifuwo na zwiṅwe zwipuka (animals)' (livestock and other animals). 'zwifuwo' follows the Small Livestock precedent, 'zwiṅwe zwipuka' covers pets and other animals, and the English word in brackets settles the meaning. 'mulambo' (river) was too narrow for watercourse, so it is now 'nḓila ya maḓi a elelaho (watercourse)' (a channel of flowing water), which covers rivers, streams and channels. 'let it pool' was 'stay gathering', which is vague. It is now 'a ime fhethu huthihi a ite tshidzivha (pool)' (stand in one place and form a pool). There are still exactly three destinations, in the English order: tshiṱaraṱa (street), drain, watercourse. Each is marked with 'kha'. Each of the four bans keeps its own 'ni songo': connect, spray, pool, run off. The order of ideas matches the English. 'mipayipi' is kept as the deck already spells it.

Major problem is real. 'zwifuwo na zwiṅwe' narrowed 'animals' to livestock and added an 'other' that is not in the English. Both are removed, so the text is now the single general term 'zwipuka' (animals, as the deck already uses it in 'u ṱanza zwipuka' for 'washing animals'), followed by the English gloss in brackets so it cannot be read as plants. The minor problem is also real. 'fhethu haṋu' became 'nga nnḓa ha mukano wa fhethu haṋu (property)', which means 'beyond the boundary of your premises' and brings back the run-off-the-property boundary meaning. Nothing else changed. All four prohibitions (connect, spray, pool, run off) keep their own negative 'ni songo', and the drain and watercourse wording is unchanged.

checkRounds.text: Thivhelani uri maḓi o shumiswaho u ṱanzwa (washwater) a kwame vhathu kana zwifuwo na zwiṅwe zwipuka (animals). Ni songo ṱumanya maḓi ayo na mipayipi ya maḓi a u nwa, ni songo a ṱhasha (spray), ni songo tendela uri a ime fhethu huthihi a ite tshidzivha (pool), kana ni songo tendela uri a elele a bva fhethu haṋu a ye kha tshiṱaraṱa, kha mugodi wa u elisa maḓi (drain) kana kha nḓila ya maḓi a elelaho (watercourse).
checkRounds.backTranslation: Be aware that water that has been used for washing (washwater) must not touch people or livestock and other plants/animals (animals) [?]. Do not mix its water with the pipes of drinking water, do not spray it (spray), do not allow it to stand in one place and make a pool (pool), or do not allow it to flow out from your place and go to the street, to the ditch for draining water (drain) or to the path of flowing water (watercourse).

problems.issue: The open problem is not resolved. The animals exposure route is still carried by 'zwiṅwe zwipuka (animals)', and the blind back-translator again read 'zwipuka' as 'plants/animals [?]'. The word is still ambiguous without the bracketed English gloss. The draft also changes 'animals' to 'livestock (zwifuwo) and other zwipuka'. That narrows the main term to farm animals and adds an 'other' that is not in the English. Pets and wildlife depend entirely on the ambiguous word. Use one unambiguous general term for animals (for example 'phukha' or 'zwipuka' only with an unmistakable animal term) and drop 'other'. As written, a reader could take the instruction as 'people, livestock and other plants'.

'property' is rendered as 'fhethu haṋu' ('your place'). This slightly weakens the boundary meaning of 'run off the property'. The 'watercourse' check is fine: 'nḓila ya maḓi a elelaho' ('path of flowing water') covers rivers, streams and channels and does not narrow it. The negations and prohibitions (connect, spray, pool, run off) keep their scope and sequence.

checkRounds.text: Thivhelani uri maḓi o shumiswaho u ṱanzwa (washwater) a kwame vhathu kana zwipuka (animals). Ni songo ṱumanya maḓi ayo na mipayipi ya maḓi a u nwa, ni songo a ṱhasha (spray), ni songo tendela uri a ime fhethu huthihi a ite tshidzivha (pool), kana ni songo tendela uri a elele a bva nga nnḓa ha mukano wa fhethu haṋu (property) a ye kha tshiṱaraṱa, kha mugodi wa u elisa maḓi (drain) kana kha nḓila ya maḓi a elelaho (watercourse).
checkRounds.backTranslation: Take note that water that has been used for washing (washwater) must not touch people or animals (animals). Do not mix that water with pipes of water for drinking, do not spray it (spray), do not allow it to stand in one place and make a pool (pool), or do not allow it to flow out beyond the boundary of your place (property) and go to the street, to a ditch for draining water (drain) or to a path of flowing water (watercourse).

problems.issue: The open problem is resolved. 'zwipuka (animals)' now reads as animals, and the retained English gloss removes the ambiguity. 'nḓila ya maḓi a elelaho (watercourse)' means any path of flowing water, so it does not narrow 'watercourse' to rivers. All four prohibitions keep their scope: no contact with people or animals, no connection to drinking-water plumbing, no spraying, no pooling, and no runoff off the property into a street, drain or watercourse. There are no modality changes, omissions or additions, and the retained English terms sit in grammatical bracketed glosses. The back-translator's 'Take note that...' for 'Thivhelani' is a loose reading, but it still carries the prohibition.

'fhethu haṋu (property)' means 'your place' and adds a possessive that the English 'the property' lacks. 'mugodi wa u elisa maḓi (drain)' means a ditch for draining water and leans toward an open ditch. English 'drain' also covers a stormwater drain or pipe, though the bracketed '(drain)' limits the narrowing. Neither point changes the safety meaning.

resolvedCheckerNotes: major/number-species: The animals referent may be wrong. English says 'people or animals'. The draft says 'vhathu kana zwipuka', and the blind back-translator read 'zwipuka' as 'plants', not 'animals'. If 'zwipuka' does not clearly mean animals, the protection is aimed at the wrong group. Animals are a named exposure route in this safety instruction. I am not certain of the Venda lexicon here, so a Venda-speaking reviewer should confirm the word. The independent back-translation is evidence that a reader could take it as plants.
revisionNotes: All four prohibitions retained. Words for spray (ṱhasha) and drain (mutsiko wa maḓi) are low-confidence and need reviewer attention.

r1: English gloss added after 'ṱhasha' because the back-translation read it as 'spill' and the spraying prohibition must be unambiguous. Other prohibitions unchanged. A facilitator should also check 'mutsiko wa maḓi' for 'drain' (back-translation marked it [?]) and 'ndilani' (road, missing the diacritic if it means the road).

r2: Real problem confirmed: final item lacked a repeated 'ni songo', so 'kana a tendela' could read as permission to let it run off; now 'kana ni songo a tendela ...'. Also 'fhirise' changed to 'fhire' (plain 'run off/pass'). Two additional fixes beyond the checker: (1) 'maḓi a u ṱanza' risks reading as 'play water' (the blind back-translator saw this); replaced with 'maḓi o shumiswaho hayani' (used household water), the precedent term in the s21 learner draft, which covers washwater. (2) 'mutsiko wa maḓi' (read as 'water source') replaced by 'mugodi wa u elisa maḓi (drain)' per the checker. 'zwipuka' is kept as 'animals'; the back-translator's 'plants' reading is mistaken (plants would be 'zwimela'), but a Venda facilitator should confirm.

opus: The reported problem is real. 'maḓi o shumiswaho hayani' adds 'at home', which narrows the prohibition, and it loses the idea of washing. The fix drops 'hayani' and uses 'maḓi o shumiswaho u ṱanzwa' (water used for washing) with an English gloss. The earlier 'maḓi a u ṱanza' was misread as play water, so the gloss is kept and a facilitator should confirm the verb. The term is placed in the first sentence so the referent of 'contact' is clear, and 'ayo' refers back to it in the second. 'a fhire' (pass by) becomes 'a elele a bva' (flow out from), which matches 'run off the property'. All four prohibitions keep a repeated 'ni songo', so the scope of each negation stays exact.

followUpEdits.reason: The A-frame check is to turn the frame round so the legs swap places and read the mark again. 'I shandukedzeni' (from shanduka, change) reads as 'change it' and occurs nowhere else in the course. Two earlier repairs used the manual's verb 'monisa' ('I monisani', then 'Monisani A-frame'); two separate blind readers took it as 'show' (as if from 'vhonisa'), and the independent check found no confirmation outside three machine-drafted manual lines (content/manual/ve/07 'Monisani furemu', content/manual/ve/11 'Monisani tshibikisi' for 'Turn the cooker'). The course's other verb for turning something is 'rembulusa': lib/course-translation-drafts-ve-soil-health.ts 'Engedzani dry carbon material i ngaho straw nahone ni i rembuluse' (Add more dry carbon material like straw and turn the heap) and 'Litshani u rembulusa heap' (Stop turning it), the Soil deck slides 11, 13 and 20 ('ni i rembuluse'), and lib/course-translation-drafts-ve-reading-landscape.ts 'tshithu tshi sa rembuluswi' (anything permanent, i.e. not moved). A blind reader in this batch rendered Soil slide 20's 'ni i rembuluse' as 'turn it'. S12t names the frame instead, with the plain plural imperative that slide 23 of this deck uses ('Fhaṱani A-frame', build an A-frame). Only one of S12s and S12t will be applied.

currentTarget.provenance: Bounded deck-only machine draft (Soil/Water ordinary-prose completion, 4–5 October 2026): drafted, blind back-translated and semantically checked by separate AI agents; difficult technical English retained. Unreviewed; not fluent or local farming approval.

targetFieldChanges.backTranslation: A Swale Can Allow Water to Enter
revisionNotes: Under 45 characters.

targetFieldChanges.sourceEnglish: This picture shows a level contour swale as a concept. Water may spread along the trench and soak in where the soil allows it.

currentTarget.text: Xifaniso lexi xi kombisa xisele (swale) lexi ringaneke eka khanthura (contour) tani hi xifaniso xa miehleketo. Mati ma nga hangalala hi ku landza mugodi ni ku nghena laha misava yi pfumelelaka kona.
currentTarget.provenance: Bounded deck-only machine draft (Soil/Water ordinary-prose completion, 4–5 October 2026): drafted, blind back-translated and semantically checked by separate AI agents; difficult technical English retained. Unreviewed; not fluent or local farming approval.

targetFieldChanges.backTranslation: This picture shows a swale (swale) that is level on the contour (contour) as a picture of ideas. Water can spread out by following the ditch and entering where the soil allows it.
revisionNotes: 'concept' follows learner 'xifaniso xa miehleketo'.
r1: 'may' now uses the potential 'ma nga + verb' pattern ('hangalala').

targetFieldChanges.sourceEnglish: It does not show how deep moisture reaches on your land. Check the soil, slope and overflow route before building.

currentTarget.text: A xi kombisi leswaku ku tsakama ku nghena ehansi ku fika kwihi emisaveni ya wena. Kambela misava, ku rhelela ni ndlela ya mati lama tlulaka u nga si aka.
currentTarget.provenance: Bounded deck-only machine draft (Soil/Water ordinary-prose completion, 4–5 October 2026): drafted, blind back-translated and semantically checked by separate AI agents; difficult technical English retained. Unreviewed; not fluent or local farming approval.

targetFieldChanges.backTranslation: It does not show how far down the wetness enters in your soil. Inspect the soil, the slope and the path of the overflowing water before you build.
revisionNotes: 'moisture' = ku tsakama (learner precedent); 'how deep' rendered as how far down.
r1: 'overflow' now 'mati lama tlulaka' (water that goes over), consistent with the deck's use of 'tlula' for overtopping.

targetFieldChanges.sourceEnglish: The Downhill Berm

currentTarget.text: Khurhana ra Misava (Berm) ra le Hansi
currentTarget.provenance: Bounded deck-only machine draft (Soil/Water ordinary-prose completion, 4–5 October 2026): drafted, blind back-translated and semantically checked by separate AI agents; difficult technical English retained. Unreviewed; not fluent or local farming approval.

targetFieldChanges.backTranslation: Mound of Soil (Berm) on the Lower Side
revisionNotes: berm with gloss per learner precedent.

targetFieldChanges.sourceEnglish: The excavated soil forms a berm on the downhill side. It is where trees may be planted when the site design is suitable.

currentTarget.text: Misava leyi celiweke yi endla khurhana ra misava (berm) etlhelweni ra le hansi. I ndhawu leyi mirhi yi nga byariwaka kona loko dizayini ya ndhawu yi fanerile.
currentTarget.provenance: Bounded deck-only machine draft (Soil/Water ordinary-prose completion, 4–5 October 2026): drafted, blind back-translated and semantically checked by separate AI agents; difficult technical English retained. Unreviewed; not fluent or local farming approval.

targetFieldChanges.backTranslation: The soil that has been dug makes a mound of soil (berm) on the lower side. It is a place where trees may be planted when the design of the site is suitable.
revisionNotes: Reuses learner wording almost verbatim.

targetFieldChanges.sourceEnglish: Trees may draw on moisture stored in nearby soil after rain; the result varies by site.

currentTarget.text: Mirhi yi nga tirhisa ku tsakama loku hlayisiweke emisaveni ya kusuhi endzhaku ka mpfula; mbuyelo wu hambana hi ndhawu.
currentTarget.provenance: Bounded deck-only machine draft (Soil/Water ordinary-prose completion, 4–5 October 2026): drafted, blind back-translated and semantically checked by separate AI agents; difficult technical English retained. Unreviewed; not fluent or local farming approval.

targetFieldChanges.backTranslation: Trees can use the moisture that is kept in the nearby soil after rain; the result differs by site.
revisionNotes: Qualification 'may' kept as 'yi nga'; 'varies by site' = wu hambana hi ndhawu.

targetFieldChanges.sourceEnglish: Storms Need a Safe Overflow

currentTarget.text: Mpfula ya matimba yi lava ndlela yo tlula yo hlayiseka
currentTarget.provenance: Bounded deck-only machine draft (Soil/Water ordinary-prose completion, 4–5 October 2026): drafted, blind back-translated and semantically checked by separate AI agents; difficult technical English retained. Unreviewed; not fluent or local farming approval.

targetFieldChanges.backTranslation: Strong rain needs a way to pass safely
revisionNotes: About 50 characters, slightly over the 45 aim; 'need' carried by the colon structure.
r1: Restores 'need' (swi lava) and a safe overflow route; about 47 characters, slightly over the 45 aim to keep both 'need' and 'safe'.

r2: Real problem: 'swidzedze' was read as 'dams' and the deck's own word for a heavy storm is 'mpfula ya matimba' (s07.p0). Replaced the subject only; 'ndlela yo tlula yo hlayiseka' kept. Heading is a little over 45 characters. The learner draft elsewhere uses 'xidzedze' for storm flow, so a Xitsonga reviewer should confirm which word they prefer.

targetFieldChanges.sourceEnglish: Assess the Overflow Before Digging

currentTarget.text: Kambela ndlela yo tlula u nga si cela
currentTarget.provenance: Bounded deck-only machine draft (Soil/Water ordinary-prose completion, 4–5 October 2026): drafted, blind back-translated and semantically checked by separate AI agents; difficult technical English retained. Unreviewed; not fluent or local farming approval.

targetFieldChanges.backTranslation: Inspect the overflow path before you dig
revisionNotes: About 48 characters, just over the 45 aim.
r1: Overflow expressed as 'ndlela yo tlula' (same as s06.h); about 37 characters, under the 45 target.

targetFieldChanges.sourceEnglish: A swale needs a planned overflow route for heavy rain. Check it before digging.

currentTarget.text: Xisele xi lava ndlela leyi kunguhatiweke yo humesa mati lama tlulaka loko mpfula ya matimba yi na. Yi kambele u nga si cela.
currentTarget.provenance: Bounded deck-only machine draft (Soil/Water ordinary-prose completion, 4–5 October 2026): drafted, blind back-translated and semantically checked by separate AI agents; difficult technical English retained. Unreviewed; not fluent or local farming approval.

targetFieldChanges.backTranslation: A swale needs a planned way to let out water that overflows when heavy rain falls. Inspect it before you dig.
revisionNotes: Reuses 'ndlela ya mati lama taleke' from slide 6 drafts.
r1: Overflow now 'mati lama tlulaka'.

targetFieldChanges.sourceEnglish: Water may go to another swale or a dam only when a site assessment shows that the route, outlet and receiver can take the flow without damage.

currentTarget.text: Mati ma nga ya eka xisele xin’wana kumbe damu ntsena loko nkambelo wa ndhawu wu kombisa leswaku ndlela, ndhawu yo humesa mati ni leswi ma amukelaka swi nga kota ku khoma mati lama khulukaka handle ka ku onhaka.
currentTarget.provenance: Bounded deck-only machine draft (Soil/Water ordinary-prose completion, 4–5 October 2026): drafted, blind back-translated and semantically checked by separate AI agents; difficult technical English retained. Unreviewed; not fluent or local farming approval.

targetFieldChanges.backTranslation: Water may go to another swale or a dam only when the site inspection shows that the path, the place for letting water out and what receives it can hold the water that flows without being damaged.
revisionNotes: 'only when' = ntsena loko; receiver rendered 'xo ma amukela'.
r1: Route, outlet and receiver are now three clear items ('leswi ma amukelaka' covers swale or dam); removed the duplicated 'amukela'; 'ntsena loko' and 'handle ka ku onhaka' kept.

targetFieldChanges.sourceEnglish: Roots help hold soil along a planted contour line.

previousTarget.text: Timitsu ti pfuna ku khoma misava eka layini ya contour leyi byariweke.
previousTarget.provenance: Bounded deck-only machine draft independently checked for source meaning; difficult technical English retained. Not fluent or local farming approval.

currentTarget.text: Timitsu ta swimilana ti pfuna ku khoma misava eka layini ya khanthura (contour) leyi byariweke — layini leyi nga na ku tlakuka ko fana ndlela hinkwayo, leyi tsemakanyaka ndhawu yo rhelela, a yi rhelelanga ehansi.
currentTarget.provenance: Bounded deck-only machine draft (Soil/Water ordinary-prose completion, 4–5 October 2026): drafted, blind back-translated and semantically checked by separate AI agents; difficult technical English retained. Unreviewed; not fluent or local farming approval.

targetFieldChanges.backTranslation: Swales of growing [?] help to hold the soil on a contour line that has been marked — a line that has the same rise/height all along the way, that cuts across a sloping place, that does not slope downward.
revisionNotes: contour kept as technical term; short gloss added so 'across the slope, not down it' is explicit per the rules.
r1: Uses 'khanthura (contour)' as on s02-s04 and states both level (same height along the whole line) and across-the-slope, mirroring s03.p0.

r2: Real problem. 'Timitsu' was read as 'trees', so I added 'ta swimilana' (of plants) to fix 'roots'. 'Leyi byariweke' now follows 'layini ya khanthura' so that 'planted' qualifies the line. The geometry gloss is kept: same height all along the line, across the slope, not down it. 'Swimilana' follows the checker's suggestion, so a reviewer should confirm it.

targetFieldChanges.sourceEnglish: Choose erosion controls with local advice; steep land needs a site assessment.

currentTarget.text: Hlawula ndlela yo sivela ku kukuleka ka misava hi ku tirhisa ntsundzuxo wa laha kaya; ndhawu yo rhelela ngopfu yi lava nkambelo wa ndhawu.
currentTarget.provenance: Bounded deck-only machine draft (Soil/Water ordinary-prose completion, 4–5 October 2026): drafted, blind back-translated and semantically checked by separate AI agents; difficult technical English retained. Unreviewed; not fluent or local farming approval.

targetFieldChanges.backTranslation: Choose a way to prevent soil erosion by using the advice of a local [person]; a very sloping area requires an inspection of the site.

harmonized.reason: 'local advice' now uses 'ntsundzuxo' (as on s20) rather than 'xitsundzuxo'; 'laha kaya' already matches the FIXED units.
harmonized.previousText: Hlawula ndlela yo sivela ku kukuleka ka misava hi ku tirhisa xitsundzuxo xa laha kaya; ndhawu yo rhelela ngopfu yi lava nkambelo wa ndhawu.

targetFieldChanges.sourceEnglish: Design the Spillway Before the Wall

currentTarget.provenance: Bounded deck-only machine draft (Soil/Water ordinary-prose completion, 4–5 October 2026): drafted, blind back-translated and semantically checked by separate AI agents; difficult technical English retained. Unreviewed; not fluent or local farming approval.

targetFieldChanges.backTranslation: Design a Spillway Before You Build a Wall
revisionNotes: 'rirhangu' = wall; spillway kept as technical term.

targetFieldChanges.sourceEnglish: Dam and Spillway: A Concept

currentTarget.text: Damu na Spillway: Xifaniso xa Miehleketo
currentTarget.provenance: Bounded deck-only machine draft (Soil/Water ordinary-prose completion, 4–5 October 2026): drafted, blind back-translated and semantically checked by separate AI agents; difficult technical English retained. Unreviewed; not fluent or local farming approval.

targetFieldChanges.backTranslation: Dam and Spillway: A Picture of Ideas
revisionNotes: Concept = xifaniso xa miehleketo (learner precedent).

targetFieldChanges.sourceEnglish: Design the spillway before the wall — an overtopped wall can breach catastrophically.

currentTarget.text: Dizayina spillway u nga si aka rirhangu — rirhangu leri mati ma tlulaka ehenhla ka rona ri nga tshoveka hi ndlela ya khombo lerikulu.
currentTarget.provenance: Bounded deck-only machine draft (Soil/Water ordinary-prose completion, 4–5 October 2026): drafted, blind back-translated and semantically checked by separate AI agents; difficult technical English retained. Unreviewed; not fluent or local farming approval.

targetFieldChanges.backTranslation: Design a spillway before you build a wall — a wall that water passes over the top of may be broken in a way of great danger.
revisionNotes: Only the deliberate term spillway retained.

targetFieldChanges.sourceEnglish: Catchment runoff is one input. A suitably qualified person must assess the site, dam and spillway design before construction.

currentTarget.text: Mati lama khulukaka ku suka eka ndhawu yo hlengeleta mati (catchment runoff) i xin’we xa swilo leswi tirhisiwaka eka dizayini. Munhu loyi a nga na swidyondzo leswi faneleke u fanele ku kambela ndhawu, dizayini ya damu na ya spillway ku nga si sungula ku aka.
currentTarget.provenance: Bounded deck-only machine draft (Soil/Water ordinary-prose completion, 4–5 October 2026): drafted, blind back-translated and semantically checked by separate AI agents; difficult technical English retained. Unreviewed; not fluent or local farming approval.

targetFieldChanges.backTranslation: Water that flows from the place for collecting water (catchment runoff) is one of the things that are used in the design. A person who has the suitable qualifications must inspect the site, the design of the dam and of the spillway before building starts.
revisionNotes: 'must' = u fanele; 'one input' rendered as one of the things used in the design.
r1: 'before construction' now impersonal ('ku nga si sungula ku aka'), no switch to 'you'.

targetFieldChanges.sourceEnglish: Care for the Dam and Its Banks

targetFieldChanges.backTranslation: Look after the dam and its sides
revisionNotes: Banks rendered as mintlhelo (sides/edges); no established bank term in the deck, so facilitators should check it.

revisionNotes: First flush kept as the technical term; concept rendered as miehleketo, following the deck precedent.
r1: 'First flush' translated as on s15.h; 'A Concept' as 'Xifaniso xa Miehleketo' like other concept slides. About 53 characters, within 1.8 times the English but over the 45 aim.

targetFieldChanges.sourceEnglish: A first-flush diverter keeps early roof runoff out of the tank.

currentTarget.text: First-flush diverter yi sivela mati ya le sunguleni lama khulukaka lwangwini ku nghena etankini.
currentTarget.provenance: Bounded deck-only machine draft (Soil/Water ordinary-prose completion, 4–5 October 2026): drafted, blind back-translated and semantically checked by separate AI agents; difficult technical English retained. Unreviewed; not fluent or local farming approval.

targetFieldChanges.backTranslation: A first-flush diverter prevents the water of the beginning flowing on the roof from entering the tank.
revisionNotes: HOLD translated.

currentTarget.provenance: Bounded deck-only machine draft (Soil/Water ordinary-prose completion, 4–5 October 2026): drafted, blind back-translated and semantically checked by separate AI agents; difficult technical English retained. Unreviewed; not fluent or local farming approval.

targetFieldChanges.backTranslation: Adjust its size according to your roof and look after it; the water that comes afterwards still needs to be checked for safety.
revisionNotes: Wording follows the learner precedent for size and maintain. Still is ma ha lava; safety check is ku kamberiwa vuhlayiseki.

targetFieldChanges.sourceEnglish: Keep Stored Water Protected

currentTarget.text: Sirhelela mati lama hlayisiweke
currentTarget.provenance: Bounded deck-only machine draft (Soil/Water ordinary-prose completion, 4–5 October 2026): drafted, blind back-translated and semantically checked by separate AI agents; difficult technical English retained. Unreviewed; not fluent or local farming approval.

targetFieldChanges.backTranslation: Protect the stored water
revisionNotes: HOLD translated.

targetFieldChanges.sourceEnglish: Used household water can contain germs, salts, cleaning products and other substances. Guidance does not define every source in the same way.

currentTarget.text: Mati lama tirhisiweke ekaya ma nga va na swilo leswitsongo leswi vangaka vuvabyi, munyu, swilo swo basisa ni swilo swin’wana. Swiletelo a swi hlamuseli swihlovo hinkwaswo hi ndlela yin’we.
currentTarget.provenance: Bounded deck-only machine draft (Soil/Water ordinary-prose completion, 4–5 October 2026): drafted, blind back-translated and semantically checked by separate AI agents; difficult technical English retained. Unreviewed; not fluent or local farming approval.

targetFieldChanges.backTranslation: Water that has been used at home can have small things that cause disease, salt, cleaning things and other things. The guidelines do not explain all sources in one way.
revisionNotes: Existing second sentence from the learner draft is reused verbatim.

targetFieldChanges.sourceEnglish: South African guidance differs on kitchen water and laundry water. Do not include toilet water, water from nappies, washing a sick person or washing animals in a reuse plan. Do not reuse water containing harmful chemicals.

currentTarget.text: Swiletelo swa Afrika-Dzonga swa hambana hi mati ya le khixini ni mati yo hlantswa swiambalo. U nga katsi mati ya thoyilete, mati ya tinapi, mati yo hlantswa munhu loyi a vabyaka kumbe mati yo hlantswa swiharhi eka pulani yo tirhisa nakambe. U nga tirhisi nakambe mati lama nga na swilo swa khemikhali leswi nga ni khombo.
currentTarget.provenance: Bounded deck-only machine draft (Soil/Water ordinary-prose completion, 4–5 October 2026): drafted, blind back-translated and semantically checked by separate AI agents; difficult technical English retained. Unreviewed; not fluent or local farming approval.

targetFieldChanges.backTranslation: The South Africa guidelines differ for kitchen water and water for washing clothes. Do not include toilet water, nappy water, water for washing a person who is sick, or water for washing animals in a plan for reuse. Do not reuse water that has chemical things that are dangerous.
revisionNotes: First sentence reused from the learner draft. Toilet as thoyilete and nappies as tinapi are loanwords I could not confirm; flag them for review.

targetFieldChanges.sourceEnglish: Before any reuse, ask the municipality and a qualified local sanitation adviser to check the exact source, the household's water and sanitation services, the intended use and the site.

currentTarget.text: U nga si tirhisa nakambe, kombela masipala ni mutsundzuxi wa laha kaya wa sanitation loyi a nga ni vuswikoti lebyi faneleke leswaku va kambela xihlovo lexi kongomeke, vukorhokeri bya mati ni sanitation bya muti, leswi u kunguhateleke ku tirhisa mati ha swona ni ndhawu.
currentTarget.provenance: Bounded deck-only machine draft (Soil/Water ordinary-prose completion, 4–5 October 2026): drafted, blind back-translated and semantically checked by separate AI agents; difficult technical English retained. Unreviewed; not fluent or local farming approval.

targetFieldChanges.backTranslation: Before you use [it] again, ask the municipality and a local sanitation advisor who has the suitable skill to inspect the direct source, the water and sanitation service of the household, which you have planned to use the water for, and the site.

harmonized.previousText: U nga si tirhisa nakambe, kombela masipala ni mutsundzuxi wa le ndhawini wa sanitation loyi a nga ni vuswikoti lebyi faneleke leswaku va kambela xihlovo lexi kongomeke, vukorhokeri bya mati ni sanitation bya muti, leswi u kunguhateleke ku tirhisa mati ha swona ni ndhawu.

targetFieldChanges.sourceEnglish: If this advice is unavailable or unclear, do not reuse the water. Soil and mulch do not disinfect wastewater.

currentTarget.provenance: Bounded deck-only machine draft (Soil/Water ordinary-prose completion, 4–5 October 2026): drafted, blind back-translated and semantically checked by separate AI agents; difficult technical English retained. Unreviewed; not fluent or local farming approval.

targetFieldChanges.backTranslation: If this advice is not available or is not understood well, do not use the water again. Soil and mulch do not kill the small things that cause disease in the dirty water that has been used (wastewater).

harmonized.reason: 'wastewater' had two renderings ('mati ya vulongo' here, 'mati lama thyakeke lama tirhisiweke (wastewater)' on s21); the clearer descriptive phrase is now used in both.

followUpEdits.text: Sivela leswaku vanhu kumbe swiharhi swi nga khumbani ni mati yo hlantswa. checkNotes: minor: Unchanged opening 'Sivela leswaku vanhu kumbe swiharhi swi nga khumbani ni mati yo hlantswa' (blind-reader flag on a possible double negative). Read literally it is 'Prevent that people or animals do not touch the washwater', and the same slide's heading uses the positive complement 'Sivela ku khumbana ni ku thyakisiwa' (Prevent contact and pollution). It is not a demonstrable meaning error: negative purposive clauses are common in the manual (e.g. 05-animal-systems.md:164 'leswaku tinyoxi ti nwa ti nga nweli' = EN 'so bees can drink without drowning'), so it can be read as 'guard so that they do not touch', and the heading and the next sentences fix the intended meaning. But it is elliptical (no object after 'sivela') and not course idiom: the manual's own pattern is sivela + noun + ku + positive verb (08-soil.md:140 'ku sivela vulongo ku hisa timitsu' = EN 'stops the manure burning roots'; 05-animal-systems.md:99 'mikhuva leyi sivelaka mavabyi ku nghena' = EN 'habits that keep disease off your farm'; 12-glossary.md:14 'ku sivela mavabyi na swivungu swo onha ku nghena epurasini'), 0 of the 24 manual uses of 'sivela' take 'leswaku' + 'nga', and the only other instance in the whole course is one unreviewed learner line ('lexi sivelaka mati leswaku ma nga ngheni emisaveni', food-forest). Because this is a health-safety instruction, rewording to remove the double-negative parse is recommended.

minor: Unchanged 'mati ya ku nwa' (water of drinking): the course writes 'mati yo nwa' (3 manual uses, e.g. 02-planning-your-farm.md:134 'Hlayisa vulongo kule na mati yo nwa' and 07-earthworks-and-water.md:399 'Kule na mati yo nwa' = EN 'Far from drinking water'), 'mati ya ku nwa' occurs nowhere else in the course, and the same deck's Q7 passage (s02.p3) already says 'tiphayiphi ta mati yo nwa', so the edited phrase is inconsistent within the deck. Understandable and pre-existing.

minor: Unchanged 'xikhulukelo' for 'drain' (blind-reader flag): it occurs nowhere else in the course (1 use, in this passage) and is a coinage from khuluka (flow) + -elo. The blind reader still parsed it correctly as a drain or channel, so it is understandable, but the course has an attested word for a drain or channel, 'mugerwana/migerwana' (07-earthworks-and-water.md:35 'Migerwana yo hambukisa mati' = EN 'Diversion drains'; 07-earthworks-and-water.md:339 'Cela mugerwana lowutsongo wo yisa mati exikarhi' = EN 'Dig a small channel to lead water to the centre').

followUpEdits.reason: "Sivela leswaku … swi nga khumbani" pairs "prevent" with a negative ("prevent that they do not touch"), a double negative that can read as requiring contact (found by the six-lens audit and by the earlier independent check). The course builds "sivela" with the thing blocked as object and ku + verb: content/manual/ts/08-soil.md "ku sivela vulongo ku hisa timitsu" (prevent manure from burning the roots); the slide heading already says "Sivela ku khumbana ni ku thyakisiwa". "mati yo nwa" (drinking water) is the course wording (content/manual/ts/02 "Mati yo nwa ma tshama ma basile", content/manual/ts/07 "Kule na mati yo nwa") and matches slide 2 paragraph 4 of this deck ("tiphayiphi ta mati yo nwa"); "mati ya ku nwa" occurs only here. "xikhulukelo" occurs nowhere in the course; "mugerwana" (channel, furrow) is the manual word for a dug water channel (content/manual/ts/07 "Cela mugerwana lowutsongo wo yisa mati exikarhi"). The independent check also found that 'ndhawu ya muti' (the place of the homestead) occurs nowhere else in the course and a blind reader could not tell yard from village; the course writes the property as 'ndhawu ya wena' (29 uses, for example content/manual/ts/02-planning-your-farm.md 'Hlaya ndhawu ya wena'), so that phrase is used here.

followUpEdits.reason: Off the property: in 24 of the 26 lines of the Xitsonga manual and learner drafts that use the bare 'handle ka', it means 'without / except / unless' (e.g. content/manual/ts/02 'gravity yi famba na mati handle ka pompi', without a pump; content/manual/ts/06 'handle ka loko u byala lufenisi', unless you plant a hedge), and this deck itself uses it so on Water slide 7 ('lama khulukaka handle ka ku onhaka', flow without damage). The two exceptions are the Xitsonga Soil lesson's 'swi ri handle ka heap' and 'handle ka ordinary compost heap' (out of the heap). The spatial 'outside (of)' is 'ehandle ka' in all 7 lines that use that form (content/manual/ts/03 'swi huma ehandle ka lufenisi ra wena', come from outside your fence; content/manual/ts/07 'leswi humaka ehandle ka marhangu'; Soil slides 12 and 13 of the Xitsonga deck 'ehandle ka compost heap'). With the bare form a reader may take 'ma khulukela handle ka ndhawu ya wena' as 'flow without your place'. The edit adds only the locative 'e'.

minor: Blind-reader flag 'mugerwana' (pre-existing; settled): it is not an unknown word in this course. It is the course's small channel / furrow / diversion-drain word (content/manual/ts/07-earthworks-and-water.md:35 'Migerwana yo hambukisa mati', :339 'Cela mugerwana lowutsongo', :355). It fits 'drain' well enough, framed by 'ndlela' and 'nambu'; the manual's plain 'drain' word is 'mugero/migero' (07:205, 07:207). Course attestation only, so I cannot independently confirm it as standard Xitsonga.

followUpEdits.reason: Taken alone, 'mati yo hlantswa' (water for washing) could be read as clean water for washing rather than used washwater (an earlier independent checker's minor note). On a sanitation slide the Sesotho and Tshivenda versions say 'used' explicitly ('metsi a sebedisitsweng ho hlatswa', 'maḓi o shumiswaho u ṱanzwa'). The Xitsonga Water lesson writes 'used water' as 'mati lama tirhisiweke' ('Mati lama tirhisiweke ma nga va na germs', used water can contain germs), and the manual defines greywater with the same words, for example manual 02 'mati lama tirhisiweke ku hlamba'; course counts: 'mati lama tirhisiweke' 2 in the Xitsonga lessons, 7 in the manual, 0 in the other Xitsonga decks; 'mati yo hlantswa' 1 in the Xitsonga lessons, 2 in the manual, 0 in the other Xitsonga decks, where the course always names what is washed ('mati yo hlantswa swiambalo', laundry water, also on Water slide 19). The slide keeps its verb 'hlantswa' (wash things). The next sentence still refers back with 'mati lawa' (this water).

The prohibition survives with its negative, so the meaning is intact but less exact.

minor: Pre-existing, unchanged by the edit: 'ku hlantswa' has no object. 29 of the 30 'hlantsw*' hits across the manual, lessons and decks carry an object, an object concord or a passive; slide 22 is the only bare one. The course's own greywater collocation is 'mati lama tirhisiweke ku hlamba' (manual 02:116, glossary 12:38), which also covers bath, shower and hand-basin water, while 'hlantswa' (wash things) can read as laundry and dish water only. This is a weak preference, not an error: the same deck uses 'hlantswa' for washing a sick person and animals (slide 19), and the new 'lama tirhisiweke' already fixes the real fault (clean versus used water).

minor: Pre-existing, unchanged by the edit: 'nambu' (river) alone narrows the English 'watercourse'. The course has 'xinambyana' (manual 01:135, glossary 12:18) and 'swinambyana' (02:40, 03:146, 06:38, 07:225) for streams. The meaning survives because 'ndlela' and 'mugerwana' (the course's word for drains and small channels, 07:35 and 07:339) share the list.

targetFieldChanges.backTranslation: I have placed markers at three places or more [?], which are at the same height, by cutting across my area that slopes downward.

reasons: The minimum is now 'tinharhu kumbe ku tlula' (three or more). This follows the learner precedent 'ku tlula' for 'exceeding' and replaces the unrecognisable 'ku tlurisa'. For 'same height' the draft had 'ku tlakuka loku fanaka', which checkers read as 'the same rising'. The new wording is 'leti ringanaka hi ku tlakuka' (equal in height). It uses the deck's own 'ringana' word for 'level' plus its 'ku tlakuka' for height, and '(same height)' is added because back-translation showed the native phrase is ambiguous. For the slope, 'ndhawu ya mina yo rhelela' follows the learner precedent 'ndhawu yo rhelela', with '(slope)' added so it is not read as 'slippery place'. 'Hi ku tsemakanya' (across) is kept, matching the deck's contour slides. 'Ndzi veke swikombiso' keeps the first-person checklist voice. It also matches the next unit, 'Layini leyi ndzi yi vekeke swikombiso'.

Slope (critical): 'ndhawu ya mina yo rhelela' could be read as 'slippery place'. It is now 'ndhawu ya mina leyi rhelelaka ehansi' ('my land that goes downward'). The word 'ehansi' (down) makes it mean ground that falls away, not slipping. This keeps the 'rhelela' wording used for slope across the deck (s08.p0, s09.p0, s23.p1, s24.p3). 'Across' stays as 'hi ku tsemakanya', so the contour sense (level points along a line across the fall) is kept. Same height (major): 'leti ringanaka hi ku tlakuka' read as 'equal by rising'. It is now 'leti nga eka vuhenhla byin’we' ('which are at one/the same height'), using the height noun 'vuhenhla' instead of the verb 'ku tlakuka'. Brackets (major): both English glosses '(same height)' and '(slope)' are removed because the Xitsonga now carries those meanings itself. At least three (minor): I kept 'tinharhu kumbe ku tlula' ('three or more'). The checker already accepts it as the exact 'at least three', and the change is kept to the smallest possible.

checkRounds.text: Ndzi veke swikombiso eka tindhawu tinharhu kumbe ku tlula, leti ringanaka hi ku tlakuka (same height), hi ku tsemakanya ndhawu ya mina yo rhelela (slope).
checkRounds.backTranslation: I put markers at three places or more, which are equal by rising/height (same height), by cutting across my place of sliding [?] (slope).

problems.issue: The slope phrase still has the open problem. 'ndhawu ya mina yo rhelela' is read by the back-translator as 'my place of sliding [?]', which is the same 'slippery place' misreading flagged before. The word 'slope' survives only as an English gloss in brackets. The draft therefore does not say that the points are level 'across my slope'. The contour geometry (same height along a line across the slope) is lost, so the result is a changed meaning and not just awkward wording. It needs a real Xitsonga term for a slope or incline (for example a word for ground that falls away or slopes downhill), with 'across' kept as 'hi ku tsemakanya'.

'Same height' is not conveyed by the Xitsonga alone. 'leti ringanaka hi ku tlakuka' reads as 'equal by rising/height', and the English '(same height)' is the only thing making the sense clear. The earlier problem, where 'ku tlakuka' was read as 'rising' and not 'height', is therefore only partly fixed. A word for height or elevation is needed, such as 'leti nga na ntlakuko/ku leha lokufanaka', or a phrase meaning 'at the same level or height above the ground'.

Ordinary English is left in the target sentence as bracketed glosses: '(same height)' and '(slope)'. Both are ordinary English words and neither is a retained technical term. They must be translated and the brackets removed. At the moment they cover for the two phrases that are still unclear in Xitsonga.

'at least three' is now recognisable: 'tindhawu tinharhu kumbe ku tlula' reads as 'three places or more'. The elliptical 'kumbe ku tlula' is slightly clipped, and a clearer form would be 'kumbe ku tlula tinharhu' or 'tinharhu kumbe ku tlula kuya henhla'. This is an awkwardness only. 'Points' is rendered as 'swikombiso' (markers), which is acceptable.

checkRounds.text: Ndzi veke swikombiso eka tindhawu tinharhu kumbe ku tlula, leti nga eka vuhenhla byin’we, hi ku tsemakanya ndhawu ya mina leyi rhelelaka ehansi.
checkRounds.backTranslation: I have placed markers at three places or more [?], which are at the same height, by cutting across my area that slopes downward.

problems.issue: No open problem remains. 'At least three' is now carried by 'tinharhu kumbe ku tlula' (three or more), and the back-translation recovers 'three places or more'. 'Same height' is now 'vuhenhla byin'we'. 'Across my slope' is now 'ku tsemakanya ... leyi rhelelaka ehansi' (cutting across, a downward-sloping area), so the across-not-down geometry holds. Two small awkwardnesses only. 'Hi ku tsemakanya' can read as the method of marking ('by cutting across') instead of the position of the points, and 'swikombiso eka tindhawu' ('markers at places') is a little roundabout for 'marked points'. Neither changes the meaning, so no fix is needed.

resolvedCheckerNotes: major/qualifier: The qualifier "at least three" is not expressed cleanly. The draft says "tindhawu tinharhu kumbe ku tlurisa" ("three places or ... tlurisa"). "tlurisa" is not a recognisable standard form. The back-translator could not interpret it either and marked it [?]. The reader therefore gets "three places or [unclear]" and not "three or more". The minimum is lost or garbled, which matters because three or more level points define the contour line.
revisionNotes: At least three is tinharhu kumbe ku tlurisa (deck precedent for at least). Same height is ku leha loku fanaka (deck precedent).

r1: 'same height' now 'ku tlakuka loku fanaka' (not length); 'at least three' now 'leti nga riki ehansi ka tinharhu' (not fewer than three). 'funghile' kept (mark; 'Fungha tindhawu' precedent in the learner drafts).
r2: Real problem: 'funghile' reads as 'sworn'. Replaced with 'ndzi veke swikombiso' (I have placed markers). 'At least three', same height and across my slope are unchanged.

opus: The problem is real. 'leti nga riki ehansi ka tinharhu' ('not below threes') hides the number 3 and does not agree with its noun, so 'at least three' was not recoverable. The fix makes the numeral agree with class 10 tindhawu ('tindhawu tinharhu') and adds the deck precedent for 'at least': 'kumbe ku tlurisa' (or more). Same height ('ku tlakuka loku fanaka'), across my slope ('hi ku tsemakanya ndhawu ya mina yo rhelela') and the r2 marker wording ('ndzi veke swikombiso') are kept word for word. The body is somewhat over the 1.8x length target, but exact quantity and geometry take priority.
